groups.rationale: Changing everyday lifestyle habits when settling abroad is a normative adaptation question, not whether to preserve origin culture or whether adaptation is difficult.
The pessimistic observers are adults generally; the separate elderly-observer prompt has a narrower population.
Both debate whether the State can control everything. Asking agreement with its inability or asking about its ability reverses polarity without changing the actor, total scope or capability question.
Requires selecting and justifying the world's highest-priority social, humanitarian or cultural cause, not choosing one's volunteer activity or assigning responsibility for aid.
Possibility of achieving one's objectives abroad is distinct from an always-positive experience, reasons to emigrate or ease of finding a particular job.
Both challenge the claim that books have become useless today. Generic singular versus plural and the explicit request for reasons do not change present utility, scope or audience.
Evaluates whether artistic occupations are serious professions, not whether arts belong in school or celebrities belong in politics.
Concerns elderly people's pessimistic view of youth specifically, not the broader adult population or the reliability of elders' advice.
Concerns difficulty of adapting abroad. Practical adjustment, overall foreign-residence difficulties and social integration are overlapping but not interchangeable tasks.
Both ask whether one should preserve one's cultures and traditions in a host country; reversing the two nouns changes neither the obligation nor the migration setting.
Recommends contact with compatriots while abroad; it does not require exclusive compatriot contact or assert the necessity of relationships with host-country inhabitants.
Evaluates the general claim that television viewing wastes time, without restricting the audience to children, the genre to reality TV or the activity to news avoidance.
Both ask whether cultural subjects should be excluded from school teaching. Music, drawing and theatre are illustrative examples of the same category, not additional mandatory subjects.
Asks whether other cultures can be known without travelling; neither a particular medium's usefulness nor speaking a country's language is the same prerequisite.
Evaluates cuisine specifically as a means of knowing countries' cultures, not books, travel or one's own country's diet.
Identical prompts question whether friendship is necessary for happiness. The broader phrase living one's life well is kept distinct rather than assumed to mean happiness alone.
Identical prompts ask whether living abroad is always positive; the universal qualifier and whole-experience evaluation are preserved.
Identical prompts ask whether the decline of personal postal correspondence is regrettable, including greeting cards and love letters; not whether handwriting is obsolete.
Asks whether a country can be known without speaking its language, not without visiting it or whether immigrants should know their host country.
Asks whether reading is necessary to be cultivated. Books may be useful without reading being a necessary condition of cultural attainment.
Evaluates a preference for travelling alone; this travel arrangement is not foreign residence, living alone at home or a universal travel obligation.
Identical prompts assert that relationships with host-country inhabitants are indispensable for living well abroad; both retain the same necessary condition and setting.
Requests motivations for choosing foreign residence, not a judgment that departures are often forced by lack of alternatives or that the experience is always positive.
Asks the personal importance of knowing the host country when immigrating; it does not request three pre-procedure questions specifically for Quebec.
Asks whether long foreign residence can cause forgetting origin culture; possible change over time is not a duty to preserve traditions.
Evaluates the difficulty of life abroad overall, including ongoing living conditions, rather than only adaptation or becoming socially integrated.
Asks whether integration into a foreign country is easy; social acceptance and belonging are not exhausted by practical adaptation or residence conditions.
Specifies harmful influence of reality television on young people, not all television, all screen time or video games.
Evaluates celebrities' place in politics, a particular participation and legitimacy question distinct from artistic professional seriousness or universal leadership capacity.
Asks about new consumption habits in developed countries broadly; online purchasing feasibility or organic-product availability is only one narrower aspect.
Evaluates immigrants' overall contribution to the receiving country, not immigrants' own reasons, adaptation, employment prospects or preservation of traditions.
Asks whether parents should permit children's social-network use; the source specifies neither unrestricted access nor a ban on every phone use.
Concerns young Canadian adults choosing to stay with parents because they feel comfortable there, unlike general practicality of cohabitation after age 25.
Tests the claim that elderly people always give good advice, not whether elders view youth pessimistically.
Both ask whether children should always be told the truth; punctuation and the optional opinion invitation leave the universal obligation and audience unchanged.
Asks whether living far from family is easy. Distance does not require living alone or in another country.
Both evaluate parents giving children money for good school marks. The grammatical variation des/de adds no different incentive, actor or outcome.
Asks whether working with a family member should be avoided, not whether living together is easy or whether family members are best friends.
Necessity of friends for living one's life well can include practical and social functioning beyond happiness. This genuinely close wording is kept separate from happiness-only prompts.
Asks whether family members are one's best friends; comparing relationship types is not deciding whether friendship is necessary for happiness.
Compares ease of living alone and living as a family, not geographic distance from relatives or staying with parents at a specified age.
Evaluates authoritarian parenting generally, not a specific permission, truth-telling duty or monetary reward.
Requires choosing mother tongue or host-country language for speaking with one's children abroad; this is narrower than preserving culture generally.
Asks whether every household member must do housework, a specific shared domestic obligation rather than an overall household arrangement.
Asks whether living with parents after age 25 can be practical; the age threshold and practicality framing differ from Canadian young adults staying for comfort.
Asks whether every person can adapt in a foreign country. Universal capacity does not imply that adaptation, residence or integration is easy.
Never too late to learn, no age limit for learning and possible to learn at every age express the same unrestricted lifelong-learning possibility. None narrows learning to formal studies.
Asks about banning mobile-phone use specifically at school, not prohibiting phones for children everywhere or controlling only social networks.
Evaluates parents withdrawing children from school to teach them at home, not learning everything alone through the Internet.
Requires exactly three justified questions before Quebec immigration procedures; destination, timing and enumerated response distinguish it from generic migration preparation.
Evaluates Internet's role in solidarity around disasters or current events, not social networks' overall utility or preferred volunteer activities.
Concerns doing formal studies at any age, narrower than the possibility of learning anything throughout life.
Identical prompts ask which solidarity action the speaker would like to do; personal preference is preserved rather than replaced with admiration or global priority.
Asks whether studies help professional success, not whether good marks contribute to success in life or whether university should admit everyone.
Concerns difficulty of learning a foreign language, without a learner-age limit, migration destination or prescribed learning medium.
Evaluates books as one means of knowing a country, narrower than knowing cultures without travel and different from language necessity.
Asks whether mobile phones provide the right information, an information-quality question rather than facilitating communication or choosing a favourite medium.
Identical prompts propose the same salary for everyone within a company, regardless of job; no different population, equality condition or setting.
Asks about limits of freedom of expression, not the State's ability to control everything or honesty towards children.
Asks whether teaching the curriculum is the school's priority; priority is not exclusivity, nor a decision about a particular subject or outing.
Both debate television's contribution to children's development; contribue/participe and generic singular/plural preserve medium, population and developmental outcome.
Identical prompts ask whether university should be accessible to everyone; both concern universal access without prescribing a particular tuition or admission mechanism.
Asks whether good marks can contribute to success in life. Marks are not studies generally, and life success is broader than professional success.
Asks whether everything can be learned alone online today; both universal subject scope and solitary Internet method are material.
Evaluates benefits to children of educational outings, including museums, zoos and galleries, not zoo utility generally or the place of arts in the curriculum.
Both ask whether children should be encouraged to participate in sports competitions. Statement-plus-opinion versus direct question changes neither encouragement nor competition.
Asks whether children's overall screen time is excessive across devices, not effects of one game or television genre or a particular ban.
Evaluates difficulty of combining employment and studies simultaneously, not age limits for studies or Internet's effects on work.
Allocates responsibility for helping people in difficulty between State and citizens; not a claim that NGOs alone can help the poorest.
Tests whether stopping meat entirely is necessary for good health, not whether voluntary vegetarianism is a reasonable dietary choice.
Asks whether organic-product consumption is reserved for the richest, not whether more supermarket organic goods or organic farming are desirable.
Asks whether children must be compelled to do sport, differing in modality and activity scope from encouraging sports competition.
Both evaluate increasing cosmetic surgery specifically to remain youthful; grammatical agreement jeune/jeunes changes no motive or population.
Identical prompts ask whether the State should prohibit tobacco and alcohol sales generally. They explicitly specify prohibition, unlike the State stopping its own selling.

The State is asked to stop selling alcohol and tobacco. This can mean withdrawal as a seller rather than prohibition of others' sales; the ambiguous source is not strengthened using its copied model answer.
Evaluates increasingly choosing a vegetarian diet generally, not a universal requirement to stop meat for health.
Compares city and countryside living specifically for elderly people; transport alternatives in a car-necessity debate do not preserve this population and outcome.
Identical prompts assess making people work until 70; the policy, age threshold and acceptability judgment all match.
Requests an appraisal of food and diet in the speaker's own country, not cuisine as cultural knowledge or developed-country consumption generally.
Both evaluate whether stress is stimulating, with no added workplace, duration or population constraint; only question punctuation differs.
Asks whether video games have negative effects on children. Harm can coexist with developmental benefits, so this is not the same claim as positive developmental contribution.
Asks whether earning much money is needed to be able to live, not to enjoy life or be happy.
Asks whether a good salary is necessary for happiness; a good wage, high earnings and enough money to live are different thresholds and outcomes.
Tests the universal impossibility of living without medicines, a distinct necessity claim not reducible to general diet, exercise or stress management.
Identical prompts assess social networks making new friendships easier; no expansion to all uses of networks or Internet-induced solitude.
Identical prompts ask whether doing without one's mobile phone is easy; ease is preserved rather than weakened to mere possibility.
Evaluates choosing never to watch any television, broader than avoiding televised news and different from judging all viewing to be wasted time.
Asserts Internet makes people solitary as a general causal characterization; the separate explicit possibility claim can be accepted while this generalization is rejected.
Evaluates refusal to watch televised news specifically, not rejecting all television or assessing news bulletins without that refusal.
Requests a general appraisal of television news bulletins, without stipulating avoidance or a comparative preferred-medium selection.
Explicitly asks whether Internet can make people solitary; possibility is weaker than the general causal claim, despite the historically identical answer.
Evaluates current usefulness of social networks overall, not just meeting new friends, reliable information or crisis solidarity.
Asks whether living without a telephone is possible, not whether abandoning a mobile is easy or rejecting several technologies is preferable.
Asks about present obsolescence of handwritten correspondence, not regret at the decline of personal postal communication.
Both present the same claim that mobile phones facilitate communication; omitting the explicit opinion invitation leaves the proposition unchanged.
Evaluates a personal preference to live without Internet, computers and phones, not mere feasibility of living without one device.
Asks whether mobile-phone use should be banned for children generally; a school-only ban and parental social-network permission have different scopes.
Identical prompts jointly assert that space travel is excessively expensive and useless; both concern space travel generally, not only tourism or scientific research.
Asks whether every purchase can be made online, not whether online shopping is preferable or new consumption habits are desirable.
Evaluates video games' contribution to child development, not television's contribution or whether games have any negative effects, which can coexist with benefits.

All debate the present-day necessity of a car in ordinary life: being indispensable and being able to live without one are converse formulations. No member specifies a city, country, age group, personal itinerary, ease requirement or legal ban.
Requires choosing among newspapers, radio, Internet and social networks; these explicit alternatives differ from the TV/Internet/radio choice.
All present Internet changing behaviour at work. Article, singular/plural and presence of an explicit opinion invitation do not alter the workplace transformation claim.
Requires choosing among TV, Internet and radio; it permits TV and excludes newspapers/social networks as separate options, unlike the other media-choice prompt.
Asks which citizen actions deserve admiration and why, not which action the speaker would personally like to undertake or which cause is globally most urgent.
Asks whether zoos have utility. Acknowledging benefits does not decide whether zoos should close on other grounds.
Asks whether every person can reduce their waste; individual capacity for a specific action differs from assessing national pollution measures or economic development.
Asks whether zoos should close, a normative institutional decision not identical to whether zoos have any utility.
Proposes limiting car circulation in cities, not banning car use in city centres; both degree and geographic extent differ.

In EO3's shared task of expressing a reasoned opinion, all three invite evaluation of increasing organic products in supermarkets. The bare trend and the explicit question about whether it is good preserve the same development, retail setting and evaluative task; no different action, population or constraint is added.
Asks about prohibiting car use in city centres, not merely limiting citywide circulation or making public transport free.
Identical prompts assert tourism destroys certain regions; both preserve territorial harm rather than asking reasons for national tourism development.
Asks for evaluation of actual pollution measures in one's country, not an unrestricted judgment of economic/environmental compatibility or a single proposed traffic policy.
Evaluates development of organic agriculture generally, a production-system question broader than organic goods in supermarkets or rich-only consumer access.
Identical prompts ask whether economic development and environmental preservation can coexist; same feasibility, economic scope and environmental constraint.
Asks whether the speaker expects easily to find work if moving to Canada, unlike general ease of departing to work abroad or young people's job-search disadvantage.
Asks whether athletes earn too much, a particular occupational population and excessive-pay judgment rather than uniform company pay or job difficulty.
Asks whether everyone can hold a position of responsibility; universal capability differs from personal manager-gender preference or celebrities entering politics.
Asks whether employers should permit workplace naps, a specific action not equivalent to promoting workplace wellbeing generally.
Identical prompts ask whether promoting wellbeing at work is important, without narrowing to naps, salary or retirement age.
Identical prompts rank salary as the most important aspect of a job; neither asks how much income is needed for happiness or survival.
Asks whether finding work is harder when young, an age-based comparison not a Canadian migration or overseas-work question.
Asks whether foreign departures are often caused by having no other choice, not the full range of motivations for choosing to live abroad.
Asks whether departing to work abroad is easy generally; no named country, personal Canadian job expectation or non-work migration goal is specified.
Requests reasons to develop tourism in a country, not agreement that tourism destroys certain regions.
Asks personal preference for working under a male or female manager, not whether everyone can manage or a general hiring-policy obligation.
Asks whether earning much money is necessary to enjoy life; neither merely being able to live nor needing a good salary for happiness is assumed identical.
Asks whether difficult occupations are the best paid, a descriptive pay relationship rather than a salary-equality policy or ranking salary among job criteria.
Proposes free urban public transport, a specific pricing policy rather than car necessity, traffic limitation or downtown prohibition.
Claims associations and NGOs are the only actors capable of helping the poorest; exclusive capacity and severe poverty differ from normative State/citizen responsibility for hardship generally.
Requests an open opinion about car-free living, without restricting judgment to possibility or necessity. It remains separate rather than acquiring the copied answer's feasibility constraint.
